note: Two-tier pattern registry for the v10r pattern library — the single source of truth every derived surface is built from: the README Pattern Index, the /docs/pattern-library section (catalog + one page per record), both MCP runtimes, /showcases/mcp, and Vely's pattern tool. Deep records are full emulation cards (invariants + emulation notes required); light records are index rows (pointers only). Every path is repo-relative and validated by mcp/validate-registry.ts. Records point to docs and code — they do not duplicate explanations.

patterns.title: Multi-client core (hexagonal domain modules)
patterns.summary: One backend operations layer ($lib/server/[domain]/) serves four clients — human UI, AI tools, REST API, background jobs — via thin wrappers, with zero duplicated business logic.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for this whenever a backend capability must be reachable from more than one entry point (page action, API route, AI tool, cron job). It is the foundation nearly every other v10r pattern builds on.

docs.note: The full pattern: canonical module shape, client wiring, error contract
Runtime 7-layer view showing where domain modules sit
Where each piece lives; import direction rules

code.note: Per-domain modules; canonical shape is [domain]/queries.ts + mutations.ts (+ service.ts only when orchestration spans multiple infra calls)

invariants: Domain functions must not import from @sveltejs/kit or $app/ — binding to the request cycle breaks tool and job reuse.
AI tools RETURN structured errors — never throw.
The tool manifest is fail-closed: if a tool is not in the manifest, the AI cannot call it; AI tools get a narrower permission set than the human UI.
Tools capture userId by closure — a tool never sees an unauthenticated call.
emulation_notes: Start every new project with this shape even if only one client exists yet — the second client (AI tool or cron) always arrives.
Keep adapters thin: a +page.server.ts action or +server.ts route should validate input, call one domain function, map the result.
patterns.risk: low — structural pattern, no external services

patterns.title: Runtime layers & request flow (7-layer view)

patterns.title: Component-first UI system (primitives/composites/layout, CVA, tokens)
patterns.summary: A layered component system — Bits UI → primitives (styled atoms) → composites (business logic) → layout (structural wrappers) — styled entirely through CVA → UnoCSS → design-token CSS variables.
patterns.when_to_use: Emulate when a project needs consistent UI at any scale: the layer split keeps styling decisions in one place and bans ad-hoc HTML.

docs.note: Design philosophy hub
Layer system and CVA variant rules
Token architecture (breakpoints, fluid type/space, elevation)
Styling flow and layout primitives

invariants: Never use raw HTML elements when a project component exists — raw <input>/<button>/<select> bypass the design system.
Styling flows through CVA → UnoCSS utilities → token-backed CSS variables; components never hardcode colors or spacing.
Components are zero-margin; layout is gap-based on the spacing scale.
emulation_notes: Adopt the layer vocabulary first (primitive/composite/layout) — it decides where every new component goes.
Port the token file before porting any component; components without tokens re-create the ad-hoc styling problem.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Design philosophy & three-tier theming
patterns.summary: Five content-first, accessibility-driven design principles paired with a three-tier token system (primitives → semantic tokens → component usage) flowing from src/app.css through tokens.ts into UnoCSS.
patterns.when_to_use: Read before making a visual design decision or introducing a new design token, to keep it aligned with the system's principles and token layering.
patterns.risk: low — documentation/convention only

patterns.title: Design tokens (breakpoints, fluid type/space, z-index)
patterns.summary: Centralizes breakpoints, fluid typography/spacing clamp() scales, and z-index values in a single tokens.ts file consumed by the UnoCSS theme so no component hardcodes design values.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for this when adding or changing a spacing, breakpoint, typography, or stacking-order value that should be shared across the app.
patterns.risk: low — frontend styling only

patterns.title: Tonal (surface) elevation engine
patterns.summary: A pure, SSR-safe TypeScript engine that computes each surface's relative depth (parent level + 1) via Svelte context and stamps it as a data-elevation attribute, decoupled from z-index.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a new stacked surface (menu, dialog, panel) needs a consistent tonal depth cue that survives Bits UI portals.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only, no runtime side effects

patterns.title: Primitives (~40 Bits UI wrappers)
patterns.summary: Roughly 40 styled atomic components (Button, Input, Badge, Select, Table, etc.) that wrap Bits UI headless primitives with CVA variants and design tokens.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the base building block for a new UI element instead of styling a Bits UI primitive directly.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Composites
patterns.summary: Higher-level components (Card, FormField, CommandPalette, Chatbot, Dock, etc.) composed from primitives that add business logic and feature behavior.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a UI need spans more than one primitive and carries app-specific behavior or layout.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Layout primitives (Stack, Cluster, Surface)
patterns.summary: Structural wrapper components (Stack, Cluster, Surface, PageContainer) that provide consistent spacing and layout without one-off CSS.
patterns.when_to_use: Use to arrange child elements with consistent gaps and structure instead of writing bespoke flex/grid CSS on every page.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Fluid responsive styling (UnoCSS, container queries)
patterns.summary: A UnoCSS-driven mobile-first strategy combining clamp()-based fluid typography/spacing, media-query breakpoints for page layout, and container queries for self-contained component responsiveness.
patterns.when_to_use: Apply when a component or page needs to scale smoothly across viewport sizes or respond to its own container rather than the viewport.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Tables
patterns.summary: A styled table primitive built on the primitives layer for rendering tabular data consistently across the app.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when displaying structured, row-based data anywhere in the UI.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Menus (dropdown, context, menu bar)
patterns.summary: Dropdown menu, context menu, and menu bar composites built on Bits UI for triggerable and right-click action lists.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when exposing a list of actions from a trigger button, right-click, or an app-level menu bar.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Split panes (resizable · reorderable)
patterns.summary: Resizable and reorderable split-pane primitives and composites for dividing screen space into adjustable regions.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a layout needs user-resizable or drag-reorderable panes, such as a multi-pane workspace.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Typography

patterns.summary: Demonstrates the three Superforms validation timing strategies: realtime (oninput), debounced async server checks, and onblur/server-only validation.

patterns.title: Locale routing (optional catch-all, matcher, 308 canonical)
patterns.summary: URL-based locale routing using an optional [[locale=locale]] catch-all segment and a param matcher, with the unprefixed default locale (en) 308-redirected from /en/* to keep canonical URLs.

patterns.title: Messages (Paraglide JS, ICU, compile-time)

patterns.title: Formatting & CLDR plural correctness
patterns.summary: Locale-explicit date, number, currency, percent, and relative-time formatting helpers built on the native Intl API, decoupled from the translation locale to avoid SSR/CSR hydration mismatches.

patterns.risk: low — presentation formatting only

patterns.title: DB content i18n (JSONB sidecar + `tc()`)
patterns.summary: A source-column plus JSONB-sidecar convention (e.g. name / name_i18n) for translating short database fields, resolved at read time by the tc() helper with an explicit locale argument.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a database field (title, name, summary) needs per-locale translations stored alongside the English canonical value.
patterns.risk: low — schema convention, no external services

patterns.title: Docs navigation hubs (README-per-directory convention)
patterns.summary: An AI-optimized docs tree where every directory's README.md is a navigation hub with topic tables, so agents read index → target file, never everything.
patterns.when_to_use: Adopt in any repo meant to be read by AI agents: it turns documentation from a pile of files into an addressable index.

docs.note: Root hub — the entry point of the whole convention
Example directory hub with topic tables
Second example hub (AI subsystem)

invariants: Each documentation directory has a README.md acting as a navigation hub: a 2-3 sentence intro plus a topic table showing which file covers what.
Navigation rule: start at docs/README.md and drill down through directory READMEs — read index, then target file, never everything.
emulation_notes: This is a convention, not code — emulate by writing the hubs, not by copying files.
Keep hub intros to 2-3 sentences; the topic table is the payload.
patterns.risk: low — documentation convention only

patterns.title: Pattern Index (the generated README capability map)
patterns.summary: A generated table in README.md mapping every repo pattern to the doc that explains it, the code that implements it, and the showcase page that proves it — rendered from this registry (136 rows, 20 categories, two tiers).
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the top-level discovery surface for what a reference repo can do; it is the human-readable projection of this registry, regenerated by patterns:build.

docs.note: The Pattern Index section itself (anchor #pattern-index)

code.note: Generates the README region + docs/pattern-library/ pages; --check mode gates staleness
Showcase-route cells are validated against this registry's hrefs

invariants: Coverage source of truth is mcp/patterns.registry.json — the README region between the PATTERN-INDEX markers is generated and must never be hand-edited.
Every row must point to docs AND code AND (where possible) a live proof route — a row without proof is a claim, not a pattern.
patterns:check in the validate gate blocks shipping a stale index; bun run patterns:build (or vr ref) regenerates it.
emulation_notes: Anchor the human-readable index to a machine-readable registry and GENERATE it — a hand-maintained twin drifts (this one did: its own row-count claim went stale before the generator existed).
Showcase-route cells are validated by mcp/validate-registry.ts against src/lib/showcases/registry.ts membership, not mere directory existence.
patterns.risk: low — documentation artifact

patterns.title: Agent Experience (AX) surfaces
patterns.summary: Five derived surfaces make the repo consumable by coding agents: a root AGENTS.md contract, raw-markdown doc variants with Accept negotiation, an /llms.txt URL map with in-band prior corrections, MCP tool errors that carry machine-actionable recovery steps, and a generated pattern library (README index + per-pattern docs pages) rendered from the pattern registry.
patterns.when_to_use: Adopt when a repo's primary consumers are AI agents: it turns passive docs into addressable, self-correcting surfaces without any hand-maintained duplicate content.

docs.note: The full AX layer: surfaces, derivation map, negotiation contract
The hosted MCP surface the Next-actions convention lives on

code.note: Universal agent contract at the repo root
The .md layer + Accept: text/markdown negotiation (303 + Vary + no-store)
/llms.txt built per request from the docs manifest
validate_snippet rule engine (findings are a success; input never echoed)

invariants: Every surface is derived — llms.txt from the docs manifest, .md bodies from the published registry, tool cards from shared JSON, the README Pattern Index and /docs/pattern-library pages from the pattern registry; none is hand-maintained.
Every registry-produced MCP error carries a required diag code AND a Next-actions recovery trailer — a new error branch without them is a compile error.
Content negotiation is 303 + Vary: Accept + no-store; each cacheable artifact lives at exactly one URL.
Tool results are text-only and never echo caller input beyond the bounded id reflection.
emulation_notes: Start with AGENTS.md and llms.txt — the standards that won adoption — and advertise them in-page/headers; an unadvertised llms.txt is dead weight.
Make recovery hints structural (a required parameter on the error constructor), not a style guideline reviewers must remember.
patterns.risk: low — read-only derived surfaces; no new state

patterns.title: Postgres client & connection (Neon serverless)
patterns.summary: Sets up the Drizzle client for PostgreSQL using the Neon serverless driver as the app's single database connection entrypoint.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it whenever server-side code needs a database handle to run Drizzle queries.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neon Postgres)

patterns.title: Schema & type inference (Drizzle, 14 namespaces)
patterns.summary: Drizzle table definitions split across 14 pgSchema() namespaces and re-exported from a single schema index for compile-time type inference.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when adding or changing database tables and query results need to stay type-safe end to end.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neon Postgres)

patterns.title: Queries/mutations split (reads-writes duality)
patterns.summary: Splits each domain's database access into separate queries.ts (reads) and mutations.ts (writes) modules.
patterns.when_to_use: Apply when structuring a new domain's database layer so reads and writes stay independently reusable across UI, API, and job clients.
patterns.risk: low — code organization pattern, no external dependency

patterns.title: Neo4j connection (Aura)
patterns.summary: Connects to a managed Neo4j Aura database over its HTTP Query API via fetch, with no driver, session, or connection pool.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it when server code needs to execute Cypher queries against the graph store.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neo4j Aura)

patterns.title: Graph modeling
patterns.summary: Defines how entities and their relationships are represented as nodes and edges in the Neo4j graph.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when deciding how to structure related entities, such as recommendations or knowledge graphs, that would otherwise need recursive SQL.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neo4j Aura)

patterns.title: Graph traversal
patterns.summary: Runs Cypher traversal queries, such as shortest-path and multi-hop lookups, over the modeled graph.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a feature needs to walk relationships between entities, like related-to queries or navigation paths.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neo4j Aura)

patterns.title: Polyglot freshness (Postgres ↔ Neo4j sync)
patterns.summary: Documents strategies for keeping references between Postgres and Neo4j valid, since no foreign keys exist across the two stores.
patterns.when_to_use: Apply when a delete or update in one store, such as a Postgres user or item, must propagate to or invalidate related Neo4j nodes.
patterns.risk: medium — spans two external managed services (Postgres, Neo4j)

patterns.title: Object storage (Cloudflare R2, presigned transfer)
patterns.summary: S3-compatible object storage on Cloudflare R2, accessed via @aws-sdk/client-s3 with presigned URLs for direct client uploads and downloads.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when the app needs to store or serve user files without routing large payloads through the server.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Cloudflare R2)

patterns.title: Cache (Upstash Redis, ephemeral patterns)
patterns.summary: In-memory key-value store on Upstash Redis, reached over HTTP REST, used for rate limiting, the circuit breaker, and other ephemeral counters.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a feature needs fast, short-lived state, such as counters or locks, without Postgres's durability guarantees.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Upstash Redis)

patterns.title: Dev→prod schema workflow (push-only, no migrations dir)
patterns.summary: Uses drizzle-kit push for schema changes during development and defers versioned generate/migrate SQL files until production holds real data.
patterns.when_to_use: Follow this while prototyping solo, then switch to generate+migrate before a production database with real user data goes live.
patterns.risk: low — dev-time workflow/config, no runtime dependency

patterns.title: Neon branch refresh from prod (control plane, run ledger)
patterns.summary: Resets the dev Neon Postgres branch from its production parent through Neon's control-plane API, recording each run in a ledger and surfacing it at an admin-only page.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when developers need production-like data in the dev branch on demand or on a schedule, without a manual dump and restore.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (Neon control plane), admin-only destructive op

patterns.title: DB bootstrap & seed
patterns.summary: Scripts and seed modules that populate a fresh database with baseline and sample data.
patterns.when_to_use: Run when provisioning a new environment or resetting a dev database to a known-good starting state.
patterns.risk: low — dev-time tooling, no production runtime dependency

patterns.title: Passwordless auth (magic link + OTP)
patterns.summary: Session-based authentication through Better Auth using a magic link and OTP code sent together in one email, with no passwords stored.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the primary sign-in method to avoid password-related breach risk and reset friction.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (email delivery)

patterns.title: OAuth (GitHub, Google)
patterns.summary: Sign-in via OAuth 2.0 providers, GitHub and Google, wired through Better Auth's built-in OAuth plugin.
patterns.when_to_use: Offer it alongside magic link/OTP as an alternative sign-in path for users who prefer an existing provider account.
patterns.risk: medium — external managed service (OAuth identity providers)

patterns.title: Route guards & per-route authorization
patterns.summary: Server-side guard functions that check a user's capability grants or admin status before allowing access to a route or API endpoint.
patterns.when_to_use: Use on any route or endpoint that must restrict access beyond plain authentication, including the 404-not-403 admin gate.
patterns.risk: low — application-level authorization logic, no external calls

patterns.title: Capability grants (request → approve → expire)
patterns.summary: A request-approve-expire workflow where users request a named capability, an admin approves or denies it, and pending requests auto-expire after 14 days.
patterns.when_to_use: Use in place of static roles when access to a feature, such as blog authoring, needs an auditable grant/revoke lifecycle.
patterns.risk: low — application-level authorization logic, Postgres-backed

patterns.title: Passkeys & step-up TOTP
patterns.summary: WebAuthn passkeys serve as a phishing-resistant first-factor sign-in credential, while TOTP is repurposed as a step-up check before sensitive actions, gated by a Redis freshness stamp.
patterns.when_to_use: Use passkeys to harden sign-in and step-up TOTP to re-verify identity right before a sensitive action like disabling 2FA.
patterns.risk: medium — security-critical auth factor, Redis-backed step-up gate

patterns.title: User management
patterns.summary: User account routes and server-side data access covering profile, settings, notifications, security, and GDPR data export.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when building or modifying the account area where users manage their own identity, security factors, and personal data.
patterns.risk: medium — handles GDPR-sensitive personal data

patterns.title: ALTCHA proof-of-work captcha
patterns.summary: A self-hosted proof-of-work captcha where the client solves a CPU-bound puzzle and the server verifies an HMAC-signed payload via altcha-lib.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it on public forms that need bot resistance without third-party captcha services or extra user interaction.
patterns.risk: medium — bot/abuse defense; misconfiguration or kill-switch misuse weakens protection

patterns.title: Honeypot (hidden field + min fill time)
patterns.summary: A no-interaction bot check combining a hidden form field bots tend to fill with a minimum elapsed-time threshold between render and submit.
patterns.when_to_use: Use on forms where adding a visible captcha would hurt conversion but basic bot filtering is still needed.
patterns.risk: medium — abuse-prevention layer; bypass reduces spam defense

patterns.title: Rate limiting (sliding window, fail-closed)
patterns.summary: A sliding-window rate limiter factory backed by Upstash Redis that produces per-purpose limiters (email, IP, comments, grants) and fails closed when Redis is unavailable.
patterns.when_to_use: Use whenever an endpoint or action needs abuse-resistant request throttling with predictable fail-closed behavior.
patterns.risk: medium — throttling correctness affects both abuse defense and legitimate-user access

patterns.title: AI daily token budget
patterns.summary: A per-user daily token cap stored in Redis that prevents a single authenticated user from exhausting AI quota through cost-amplification abuse.
patterns.when_to_use: Apply it to any AI-backed feature where per-user spend must be bounded before a request is served.
patterns.risk: medium — governs AI cost exposure; misconfiguration can allow spend amplification

patterns.title: Bot decision & abuse audit
patterns.summary: A shared Decision type and audit trail that lets the anti-abuse layers (captcha, honeypot, rate limits) record and explain their bot/allow decisions consistently.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a new abuse-detection signal needs to plug into the shared decision and audit-logging pipeline.
patterns.risk: medium — central point for abuse-signal correctness and auditability

patterns.title: Admin area, guards & data-table pattern
patterns.summary: The overall admin area architecture — a vertical sidebar, route guards, and a canonical data-table pattern reused across admin pages.
patterns.when_to_use: Reference this when adding a new admin page or list view that needs consistent guarding and table UX.
patterns.risk: medium — gates privileged access; guard bugs risk privilege escalation

patterns.title: GDPR data transparency (view · export · delete)
patterns.summary: A privacy aggregator that collects everything the app knows about a user into one report, backing the view, export, and delete surfaces required by GDPR.
patterns.when_to_use: Use it whenever a new domain stores personal data and must be reflected in access, portability, or erasure requests.
patterns.risk: medium — legal-compliance surface; incomplete data collection breaches GDPR obligations

patterns.title: Consent & cookies
patterns.summary: Client-side consent state and a consent banner component that gate any cookie or storage write, satisfying ePrivacy/TDDDG consent requirements.
patterns.when_to_use: Use before writing any non-essential cookie or client-side tracking value that requires prior user consent.
patterns.risk: medium — consent bugs cause non-compliant cookie writes

patterns.title: Data retention policy & purge jobs
patterns.summary: Scheduled jobs that enforce data-retention policy by purging stale records on a fixed cadence, using the shared backend jobs framework.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a new data domain needs an automatic expiry/purge cycle rather than indefinite retention.
patterns.risk: medium — retention gaps or over-eager purges both carry compliance/data-loss risk

patterns.title: Cross-device debug pairing (QR + HMAC cookie)
patterns.summary: A short-lived, single-use pairing code and QR flow that attributes a phone's anonymous pageviews to an admin's identity via an HMAC-signed cookie, without logging the phone in.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when an admin needs to test the live site on a second device and see its activity attributed on the dashboard.
patterns.risk: medium — HMAC cookie and code claiming must resist forgery/replay

patterns.title: Style picking + custom palettes
patterns.summary: A per-visitor palette, typography, and radius resolution system with a randomizer, manual picker, and optional saved custom palettes, deliberately without a site-wide brand lock.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a visitor's own style preference should drive theming instead of a fixed site-wide brand.
patterns.risk: low — cosmetic per-visitor theming, no sensitive data involved

patterns.title: Audit log, announcements, feature flags
patterns.summary: Admin-side systems for recording an audit trail of privileged actions, publishing site announcements, and toggling feature flags, all under the admin server module.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when an admin action needs to be logged, a message needs to be broadcast to users, or a feature needs a togglable flag.
patterns.risk: medium — audit integrity and flag correctness affect privileged operations

patterns.title: Feedback capture
patterns.summary: A user feedback capture form protected by the honeypot bot-detection pattern to keep submissions spam-free.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when adding a lightweight feedback channel that needs basic spam protection without a full captcha.
patterns.risk: low — non-sensitive user feedback, spam is the main risk

patterns.title: AI tool manifest & harness split (tool defs, risk metadata, registry)
patterns.summary: Tool definitions are thin wrappers whose risk-tier metadata and per-surface membership live in a registry, with harness concerns (agent loop, compaction, policy) factored out separately.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as soon as an LLM gets tools: the manifest/harness split is what keeps tool permissions auditable and surfaces honest.

docs.note: Tool calling and per-surface tool membership
Harness audit lens: loop, policy, compaction

tests.note: Drift-guards the replay map against the live tool set

invariants: Risk-tiered approval gates, not per-tool needsApproval flags — approval fatigue is reproducible; the tier rule is the working pattern.
executeDeskToolCall is the single door for mutating tool execution (one SSOT).
stepsForScopes caps agent steps per scope (read-only including desk:ask = 3, mutation = 5).
emulation_notes: The manifest is not a single file: meta maps in tools/index.ts + risk vocab in tools/_types.ts + the approval rule in policy/governor.ts together form it.
Write the drift-guard test early — it is what keeps the manifest honest as tools accumulate.
patterns.risk: high — governs what an LLM is allowed to execute

patterns.title: AI surfaces (chatbot vs deskbot split over one guard)
patterns.summary: Two AI surfaces over one shared guard: a read-only, citation-faithful chatbot (Vely) vs an agentic, mutating, approval-gated deskbot — with a showcase-only rag-demo value kept out of production paths.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when one product needs both a safe answer-bot and an acting agent: splitting the surface (not forking the stack) keeps permissions and prompts honest per surface.

docs.note: The surface split and per-surface rules
AI subsystem hub
How the deskbot integrates with the desk

showcases.note: Chatbot architecture page; the sibling deskbot page mirrors its anchor set
Deskbot architecture page; the live deskbot runs at app route /desk

invariants: The chatbot never emits a DeskEffect and never creates a proposal.
A chatbot tool never carries a desk scope; a deskbot tool always does — topology derives from manifest membership, not a scope artifact.
rag-demo is not a product surface and must not dilute the chatbot.
emulation_notes: Start with the read-only surface; add the mutating surface only with the approval gate (see deskbot-approval-gate).
Route adapters stay thin — both surfaces call the same guard then their orchestrator.
patterns.risk: high — user-facing LLM behavior and permissions

patterns.title: Deskbot approval gate (proposal → approve, plan-gated mutation)
patterns.summary: Write/destructive desk tools never mutate inside the agent loop; they return a requiresApproval sentinel that becomes a proposal (PlanCard), executed only via an approve-route replay that records the real approver and time.
patterns.when_to_use: Mandatory companion to any mutating AI tool: it converts 'the model wants to write' into an auditable human decision.

docs.note: Where the gate sits in the harness
Proposal lifecycle in the desk

invariants: The hard gate is at the tool layer — write/destructive tools return a requiresApproval sentinel; requiresApproval(risk) is the single rule.
Planning is soft guidance, not the gate — shouldRequirePlan only decides whether to instruct the model to plan.
Approval binds execution — the post-approval resume turn is filtered to read-only scopes so it cannot re-mutate.
emulation_notes: An earlier design (inline ConfirmCard with a model-minted confirmed=false→true handshake) was superseded and never shipped — do not emulate it; the proposal→approve flow is the proven shape.
Record who approved and when at the approve route — the audit trail is the point.
patterns.risk: high — the safety boundary for AI mutation

patterns.title: Layered RAG (llmwiki pointer layer over a rawrag kernel)
patterns.summary: A shared rawrag retrieve() kernel (embed → tiers → RRF fusion → drill) feeds two layers: llmwiki TLDR pointer pages as the answer surface over immutable rawrag chunks as the audit trail.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a project needs grounded answers over a corpus: start with read-only search plus citation/provenance before adding any mutating tools.

docs.note: The two-layer architecture
Corpus and ingest door
Graph tier

invariants: The kernel is never forked — a single user_id tenant filter at the chunk level is the corpus boundary; a duplicated filter would be a cross-tenant leak.
Retrieval tools close over userId via buildRetrievalTools({ userId }) — the model cannot forge identity.

Raw chunks are source truth; llmwiki is the compressed pointer layer — the model answers from wiki TLDRs by default and drills into raw chunks only when the user asks for exact wording or challenges a claim.
emulation_notes: 'nRAG' in docs is a concept name only — the code identifier is rawrag/retrieve(); do not search for an nrag module.
Build the raw layer first; the pointer layer compiles from it and can start empty.
patterns.risk: medium — external embedding/LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Retrieval ingest/search endpoints (one ingest door, /api/retrieval/*)
patterns.summary: The RAG corpus is fed and queried through /api/retrieval/* HTTP endpoints plus a unified ingest door: the app runtime and the Bun docs-ingest script share the same pure planChunks() core.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when the corpus must be maintainable from more than one runtime (app UI and scripts) without forking chunking logic.

docs.note: The ingest door pattern
Observability over the pipeline

code.note: Bun script sharing the same planChunks() door

showcases.note: Retrieval now lives as the #nrag section of the surface pages; the ingest/explorer showcases were retired

invariants: One ingest door: the standalone script reuses the app's pure planChunks() so both runtimes share one chunking implementation.
Section-parent chunks are stored with embedding = NULL so tier-1 retrieval never surfaces them.
Re-ingest is resume-safe and idempotent.
emulation_notes: Keep the chunker pure (no I/O) — that is what makes the door shareable across runtimes.
Mind embedding-provider daily quotas when re-ingesting a whole corpus.
patterns.risk: medium — writes to the corpus store; provider quotas apply

patterns.title: Chat assistant "Vely" (orchestrator, streaming)
patterns.summary: The chat-orchestrator module streams multi-provider LLM responses through Vely, v10r's floating chat assistant, using Vercel AI SDK v6.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it when a product needs a streaming, tool-capable chat UI backed by interchangeable LLM providers.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Persistent minimizable chatbot session
patterns.summary: A client-side Svelte state machine keeps Vely's conversation alive across page navigation, minimizing the panel instead of closing it when the user follows a link.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a floating chat widget must survive route changes and reloads without losing the live thread.
patterns.risk: low — client-side state only, no external calls

patterns.title: Provider registry & routing (chat/tools/vision + circuit breaker)
patterns.summary: Resolver functions pick an active chat, tool-calling, or vision LLM provider per turn and trip a Redis-backed circuit breaker on rate-limited providers.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when an app must route between multiple LLM providers by capability and needs cross-instance cooldown on failures.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Chatbot site awareness (page context)
patterns.summary: Server-resolved page context is injected as a passive block into the chatbot's prompt so deictic questions like "how does this work?" resolve to the page the user is viewing.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a floating assistant needs to ground answers in whatever public page the user currently has open.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Graph RAG pipeline (three tiers, RRF fusion)
patterns.summary: Vector-similarity chunk retrieval is combined with Neo4j knowledge-graph traversal across three parallel tiers, fused by reciprocal rank fusion, for more explainable answers.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when vector search alone misses multi-hop relationship queries that a knowledge graph can answer.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Retrieval observability (waterfall, explorer)
patterns.summary: A waterfall/step-timeline view exposes the concurrent-tier timing, provenance paths, and token breakdown behind each nRAG retrieval turn.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when developers or users need to inspect why a RAG answer was grounded the way it was, including per-tier timing and cost.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Image metadata reader (vision)
patterns.summary: A vision-capable LLM proposes title, caption, alt text, keywords, and category for an uploaded image, which a human reviews and approves before anything persists.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when uploaded media needs AI-drafted metadata but a human must confirm every field before it is saved.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Cost & usage monitoring
patterns.summary: Chat and image telemetry are merged into one admin table that derives a reference token cost at read time from a hand-maintained price table, without charging or faking a real bill.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when multiple AI surfaces need a single cross-surface view of token usage and reference spend.
patterns.risk: low — read-only admin reporting over existing telemetry

patterns.title: TOON token-efficient context format
patterns.summary: A compact, TOON-style serialization packs structured context data for LLM prompts more densely than JSON, currently implemented as a hand-rolled layout rather than the external @toon-format/toon library.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when prompt context is large structured/tabular data and token budget for the call is tight.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Deskbot (AI in the desk workspace)
patterns.summary: An agentic AI surface embedded in the desk workspace calls desk-mutating tools, with writes routed through the harness's proposal-and-approval gate.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when an AI assistant needs to act on a workspace's files and panels, not just answer read-only questions.
patterns.risk: medium — external LLM providers with quota limits

patterns.title: Agent-harness audit lens (loop/context/policy/tools)
patterns.summary: A conceptual audit lens (not a module) names which slice — loop, context, policy, or tools — owns each agent-harness primitive such as compaction, step caps, and approval gating.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when auditing whether an LLM-agent product has the harness primitives it needs and where each one is implemented.
patterns.risk: medium — governs the agent loop that drives external LLM providers

patterns.title: Image Kit (upload → AI pipeline → adjust → approve, persists nothing)
patterns.summary: A single-page toolkit that chains an AI metadata reader, frame-cropper, and embedder on one uploaded image, then discards the upload after an honest approval terminal.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as a reference for building a stateless, multi-tool AI workflow that never persists user-uploaded media.
patterns.risk: low — no persistence of uploaded media, vision-call cost is the main concern

patterns.title: Pageview collector hook (last of 14 middleware stages)
patterns.summary: A hooks.server.ts middleware stage that runs last in the 14-stage sequence and records public GET pageviews into separate anonymous and authenticated lanes only after auth and routing have resolved; sessions gain human_confirmed_at via a consent-free confirm ping so dashboards count JS-corroborated visitors, and collection is muted in dev because every environment shares one database.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it when first-party pageview logging needs to sit directly in the request hook chain instead of a third-party analytics script.
patterns.risk: low — server-side telemetry write, no external service

patterns.title: Consent-gated sessions (cookieless day-rotating id)
patterns.summary: Session identification switches between a cookie-based id under the analytics consent tier and a cookieless hash(visitorId + UTC day) id under the necessary tier, so both tiers still produce a countable session.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when session tracking must stay legally gated by consent tier (TDDDG/ePrivacy) while still counting unique sessions at the lowest tier.
patterns.risk: low — reads a consent cookie only, no external service

patterns.title: User journeys (client beacon)
patterns.summary: Page-to-page journeys are computed in Postgres with a LEAD() window function over consecutive pageviews in a session and shown as a ranked table rather than an aggregate flow diagram.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when you need real per-visitor navigation paths without merging visitors with different journeys into one misleading diagram.
patterns.risk: low — client beacon posts to a first-party endpoint only

patterns.title: Funnels
patterns.summary: Funnel conversion is computed as count(distinct session_id) per step in one grouped query, so a reload mid-funnel is deduped instead of double-counted.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when measuring step-by-step conversion through a defined sequence of pages or events.
patterns.risk: low — read-only aggregate query

patterns.title: Live events feed
patterns.summary: An unauthenticated, self-limiting SSE stream at /api/analytics/stream pushes live event-style updates for the showcase demo, using synthetic rather than production data.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as a template for a rate-limited public SSE endpoint that streams live-looking activity without exposing real user data.
patterns.risk: low — unauthenticated but self-limited (per-IP rate, connection ceiling, hard timeout)

patterns.title: Rollup & cleanup jobs
patterns.summary: Two scheduled jobs aggregate yesterday's events into a daily_page_stats table and enforce per-table retention windows (60-180 days) across the analytics tables.
patterns.when_to_use: Use this pair as the pattern for turning raw event tables into a trend-friendly daily rollup while keeping storage bounded.
patterns.risk: low — background job scoped to analytics tables, idempotent

patterns.title: Visitor "my data" transparency
patterns.summary: An authenticated "Your data" page streams cookie state, live request metadata, and a full collectUserData report so a visitor can see what analytics has captured about them.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a product needs a self-service transparency/export view satisfying a GDPR Art. 15 access request.
patterns.risk: low — read-only authenticated page, no external service

patterns.title: Router, outbox & delivery worker
patterns.summary: NotificationService.send() writes an in-app record, evaluates the settings matrix per channel, then queues outbox rows delivered by an in-process worker on containers or a cron sweep on Vercel.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the single entry point for sending any multi-channel notification instead of calling a channel provider directly.
patterns.risk: low — internal queue/dispatch, no direct external call from the router itself

patterns.title: Channel providers (email · Telegram · Discord)
patterns.summary: Email (Resend), Telegram (bot API), and Discord (OAuth2) each implement a common provider interface (send/validateConnection/getProviderName) behind their own connection and token-management flow.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when adding or maintaining an outbound notification channel that must plug into the shared router and outbox.
patterns.risk: low — outbound sends only, credentials encrypted at rest

patterns.title: In-app SSE stream & notification center
patterns.summary: A container-mode in-memory connection map pushes notifications over SSE in real time (falling back to invalidate()-based polling on Vercel serverless) and feeds a Svelte 5 runes notification-center state.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when the UI needs near-real-time in-app notification delivery without standing up a third-party pub/sub service.
patterns.risk: low — same-origin authenticated stream, connection-limited

patterns.title: Settings matrix (channel × type)
patterns.summary: The settings UI renders a channel-by-notification-type matrix backed by a form schema, letting a user toggle which channels receive which notification types.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when users need granular per-channel, per-type control over which notifications they receive.
patterns.risk: low — user-scoped preference writes only

patterns.title: Schema & delivery log
patterns.summary: The multi-channel schema adds per-user channel-connection tables, verification tokens, and push subscriptions, plus a notification_deliveries table logging per-channel send status.
patterns.when_to_use: Use as the reference schema when modeling a new channel connection or auditing delivery outcomes.
patterns.risk: low — schema/reference only

patterns.title: Jobs & scheduling (registry, runner, platform-owned cadence)
patterns.summary: A slug→execute job registry with a unified runner; cadence lives entirely in platform config (Vercel cron vs container setInterval), so switching hosts needs zero job-code change.
patterns.when_to_use: Use for any recurring or background work — the registry/runner split keeps jobs testable and host-portable.

docs.note: The full pattern including cadence ownership

code.note: Registry: slug → execute function, nothing more

invariants: The registry maps a slug to an execute function — nothing more; cadence lives in platform config, the registry has no schedule field.
Every registered job needs a vercel.json cron entry — a slug with no entry never fires.
Cron delivery is at-least-once — jobs must be idempotent.
emulation_notes: Jobs are a client of domain modules (multi-client core): a job body should call the same domain functions the UI calls.
Vercel Hobby tier rejects sub-daily cron schedules at deploy time — plan cadence accordingly.
patterns.risk: medium — touches deploy config and background execution

patterns.title: Platform scheduling (Vercel cron vs container `setInterval`)
patterns.summary: Cadence is owned entirely by platform config — vercel.json crons hitting /api/cron/[job] on serverless, or a single flat setInterval scheduler on persistent containers — so the job registry itself never changes when switching hosts.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a job must run on a schedule across more than one hosting target without duplicating scheduling logic per platform.
patterns.risk: medium — touches deploy config (vercel.json crons) and background execution

patterns.title: Registered jobs (retention, cleanup, sync, delivery)
patterns.summary: The concrete job implementations — retention sweeps, cleanup, external sync, and delivery — are idempotent slug-keyed functions run by the shared runner and manageable from an admin UI.
patterns.when_to_use: Use this catalog as the template when adding a new retention, cleanup, sync, or delivery job to the registry.
patterns.risk: low — idempotent, age-filtered deletes/syncs, admin-gated manual trigger

patterns.title: Localized manifest & installability
patterns.summary: The web manifest is served dynamically so name/description follow the Paraglide locale cookie, with maskable icons and an explicit cache header that pre-empts the hooks' no-store stamp.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when the app must be installable across locales with a manifest that stays consistent with the visitor's language.
patterns.risk: low — static/localized metadata endpoint, no mutation

patterns.title: Service-worker caching contract (HTML network-only, kill switch)
patterns.summary: The custom service worker precaches the hashed build and icons, serves HTML and __data.json network-only while never intercepting /api/* or SSE, and ships a kill switch that force-wipes caches and unregisters on a bad deploy.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when you need an installable offline shell without caching personalized HTML, plus a documented recovery path for a broken worker.
patterns.risk: medium — touches deploy config and can affect every installed client if misconfigured

patterns.title: Update flow (silent + idle toast, no auto skipWaiting)
patterns.summary: A pending service-worker update rides the next client-side navigation silently, or for navigation-less sessions surfaces one persistent reload toast after 30 minutes, and never auto-activates with skipWaiting().
patterns.when_to_use: Use when rolling out a new service-worker version without disrupting an in-progress user session.
patterns.risk: low — UI prompt only, no forced reload

patterns.title: Web push channel (declarative JSON, no PII)
patterns.summary: Web push uses one Declarative Web Push JSON payload carrying no PII (brand title, generic body, same-origin navigate path) so real content only loads after tap-through session auth, delivered synchronously and bypassing the outbox.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when adding browser push notifications that must render on iOS Safari without SW code while staying privacy-safe on lock screens.
patterns.risk: low — no PII in payload, subscriptions capped and pruned per user

patterns.title: Charts
patterns.summary: Chart.js wrapper components for standard statistical charts (bar, line, area, pie, radar, bubble, scatter) with SSR-safe canvas lifecycle handling.
patterns.when_to_use: Reach for it when a page needs a standard statistical chart type backed by Chart.js rather than a custom SVG visualization.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Plots
patterns.summary: Chart.js scatter plots and a canvas-based heatmap component for visualizing continuous or correlated data.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a dataset calls for a scatter plot or heatmap rather than a categorical chart.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Diagrams
patterns.summary: @xyflow/svelte-based flow and state diagram components with custom node types for interactive node-edge visualizations.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when building an interactive flowchart or state-machine diagram that needs draggable, connectable nodes.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Node graphs
patterns.summary: D3-powered network, tree, DAG, Sankey, and knowledge-graph layout components, rendered as SVG by Svelte while D3 only computes positions.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when visualizing relationships, hierarchies, or flow volumes between entities as a node graph.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Maps
patterns.summary: MapLibre GL components for a base map, markers, and GeoJSON choropleth overlays, using free CartoDB tiles.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when a page needs an interactive WebGL map with markers or geographic data overlays.
patterns.risk: low — frontend only

patterns.title: Timelines
patterns.summary: Timeline visualization components for displaying a sequence of dated events.

patterns.title: Desk workspace (dock layout, focus architecture, mobile projection)
patterns.summary: A full-page multi-panel workspace on a binary split-tree dock: resizable panes, drag-and-drop tabs, a panel-type registry, typed cross-panel pub/sub (DeskBus), one persisted desktop tree with total focus derivation, and a mobile chrome that is a projection over the same state — never a second layout.
patterns.when_to_use: Use for IDE-like authoring surfaces where several content types (editor, explorer, spreadsheet, AI bot) must coexist, communicate, and stay AI-drivable — and where the same workspace must work on phones without forking its state model.

docs.note: The hub: focus architecture, desk effect contract, mobile chrome, Explorer, DeskBus channels
How a new file-backed panel type joins the workspace

code.note: The whole composite: DockLayout, leaves, tab bars, mobile chrome, state modules
Split-tree state: total focus derivation (focusedLeafId → first non-empty leaf fallback), focusSeq counter
Pure tree math (split/remove/move) — kept side-effect-free and unit-tested as such
focusPanel() — the single focus writer every activation path goes through (tabs, drawer rows, AI effects, deep links)
Typed pub/sub channels between panels (context-scoped factory, not module state)
File registry domain module + DockLayoutState valibot schemas

tests.note: Gates DockLayoutState ↔ valibot schema key parity

showcases.note: The same DockLayout embedded in a Card with mobileChrome="bar" — proves the composite is not /desk-specific

invariants: The persisted DockLayoutState is always the desktop tree; mobile is a projection over it — mobile paths may focus, open, or close panels, never split or resize.
Exactly one focused panel per dock instance on every surface. Menus, AI page context, and the mobile visible panel all derive from it; every activation path writes through focusPanel().
Every DockLayoutState field must exist in DockLayoutStateSchema in the same commit — valibot strips unknown keys silently, so a missed field diverges the DB lane without an error.

No module-level $state for per-dock-instance concerns (panel menus, mobile surfaces) — context-scope them so two dock instances on one page cannot cross-talk. Singleton-ness follows the resource: per-tab resources like the visual viewport may be module singletons.
Desktop panel kebab and mobile commands sheet render the same composePanelMenus() array — a difference between them is a bug.
A desk effect that surfaces a panel leaves it visible without further interaction — overlay auto-close (focusSeq) is part of the effect, not a courtesy.
emulation_notes: Build the tree math as pure functions over a plain node type first (dock.operations.ts) and test it in isolation; wire reactivity in a separate .svelte.ts state class.
Vitest's node environment compiles Svelte in SERVER mode: factory-scoped $derived evaluates once and freezes. Any derived state you want to unit-test must be a plain function reading $state sources.
Make focus total, not optional: the stored focusedLeafId if it still resolves, else the first non-empty leaf. Consumers never handle a 'nothing focused' state while panels exist.
Bump a monotonic focusSeq on every focus write, repeats included — overlays close by watching it, which makes 'AI focused the already-visible panel' still dismiss the drawer.
Keep closed panels in the panels registry (only the tree entry is removed) — that is what makes close-undo a cheap re-attach instead of a state reconstruction.
patterns.risk: medium — persists workspace layout locally and via the file registry; no cross-user surface
